title: The Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7)
hook: the youngest shepherd is chosen, not the tall brothers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saul, the bleating sheep, and Samuel's answer. Your line was do the plain thing. Did you do one plain thing exactly as asked? Today, Samuel goes looking for the next king. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A horn of oil, and a dangerous errand. Samuel is sent to Bethlehem, to the house of a man named Jesse, because God has chosen a king from among his sons. Samuel is afraid: if Saul hears, he says, he'll kill me. So he goes with a heifer, to offer a sacrifice, and invites Jesse and his sons. The first son walks in. Eliab, the eldest. And Samuel looks at him and thinks, surely this is the one. He looks like a king. He's tall. Last time, Israel got a king who stood head and shoulders above everyone. Samuel has seen what a king looks like. This must be him.
screen: `A HORN OF OIL, TO BETHLEHEM.` → `ELIAB WALKS IN.` → `SURELY THIS IS THE ONE.`

segments.voice: And God says no. Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. Then the line this chapter turns on: "for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Even a prophet, even Samuel, judged by height. Then Jesse brings the next son, Abinadab. Not this one. Then Shammah. Not this one. The text says Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, and to each one the answer was the same: the LORD has not chosen these. So Samuel asks a question that sounds almost funny: are these all your children? And Jesse says, well, there's still the youngest. He's out keeping the sheep. Nobody thought to call him in. He wasn't even in the room. Samuel says, send and fetch him; we won't sit down until he comes. So they wait, everyone standing, for a boy to come in from the field. And when David arrives, the text does something surprising. It describes him. Ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and good to look at. The same chapter that says don't look at appearances tells us he was handsome. Some readers find that a little joke in the text: the point was never that looks are bad, only that they aren't what God goes by. And God says: arise, anoint him, for this is he. Samuel takes the horn of oil and anoints him in the middle of his brothers, and the spirit of the LORD comes on David from that day forward. The brothers in the room are passed over, and the one left in the field is chosen.
screen: `EVEN SAMUEL JUDGED BY HEIGHT.` · `SEVEN SONS, AND NOT THESE.` · `THE YOUNGEST, OUT WITH THE SHEEP.` · `HANDSOME TOO, AND THAT'S NOT WHY.` · then, large: `THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look past one appearance. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've sized up by how they look, or sound, or dress, or what they do for work. Someone you've filed away quickly. It might be a coworker, a neighbor, a relative, or you, in the mirror. Hold their face in mind. Then set the outside aside and ask: what do I actually know about their heart? What have they carried? What have they done when nobody was watching? If you don't know, just notice that. If you pray, you can hold Samuel's lesson: the LORD looketh on the heart. The bell holds the time.
David, the youngest son left out in the field, ruddy and good to look at, whom God chose because he looks on the heart, not the height.
Your line: the heart, not the height. Today, when you meet someone, notice your first judgment, and then go looking for one thing about them you can't see. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Jews read David's anointing in Bethlehem as part of the Former Prophets, and the line that God looks on the heart is studied as a teaching about not judging by appearances.

original.note: Hebrew: the heart, what God looks on in 1 Samuel 16:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: looks don't matter.
what it means: even the prophet judged by height; God chose the youngest, the one no one called in from the field.
what a scholar hears: right after the line about appearances, the text describes David as ruddy, with beautiful eyes, and good to look at.

sources.quoted: for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of the 16:7 fragment (certain in the KJV).
'Seven of his sons' is in 16:10. Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah are named in 16:6–9.
'Last time Israel got a king who stood a head above everyone' recalls 10:23 (day 732).
'Some readers find that a little joke in the text' is attributed, not asserted.
Original: לֵבָב is the form in 16:7 ('yir'eh lalevav'); confirm (vs. לֵב) and the pronunciation.
The word segment says God 'sees the heart'; the text says 'looketh on'. Acceptable paraphrase; editor check.

Editor: 'the tallest son' changed to 'the eldest son' and 'the tall brothers in their best clothes' to 'the brothers in the room' (only Eliab's height is implied, and no clothes are mentioned); 1 Samuel 17:13 added to sources because 16:1–13 never calls Eliab the eldest; 'a head above' aligned with 10:23's 'from his shoulders and upward'.
